title: Repair a node table

samples.expr: let mk = create () in let a = mk "x" [] in let b = mk "x" [] in string_of_bool (a == b)
samples.label: let mk = create () in let a = mk "x" [] in let b = mk "x" [] in string_of_bool (a == b)

samples.expr: let mk = create () in let a = mk "x" [] in let b = mk "y" [] in Printf.sprintf "%d %d" a.id b.id
samples.label: let mk = create () in let a = mk "x" [] in let b = mk "y" [] in Printf.sprintf "%d %d" a.id b.id

hints: The key needs two parts: `op`, and something that says which sources.
`List.map (fun n -> n.id) src` turns the list of source nodes into a list of their ids.
On a hit, return `n` itself. `{ n with src }` builds a copy, and a copy is not `==` to the original.

answer.code:
type node = { id : int; op : string; src : node list }

let create () : string -> node list -> node =
  let tbl = Hashtbl.create 64 and next = ref 0 in
  fun op src ->
    let key = (op, List.map (fun n -> n.id) src) in
    match Hashtbl.find_opt tbl key with
    | Some n -> n
    | None ->
      let n = { id = !next; op; src } in
      incr next; Hashtbl.add tbl key n; n
answer.explain: The key `(op, List.map (fun n -> n.id) src)` says exactly which node this is: the same op on the same sources. When that key is already in the table, returning the stored `n` hands back the one node that was built the first time, so nothing is ever built twice.
